title: Spine Surgery
summary: Decompression, fusion and spinal trauma surgery.

lessons.title: Degenerative Spine Disease

levels.kid:
Your spine is a stack of bones called **vertebrae**, like a tower of donuts. Between each bone is a squishy cushion called a **disc**, like a jelly donut. The hole in the middle of the tower holds your spinal cord and nerves.

As people get older, the cushions can dry out and flatten, and bones can grow little bumps. Sometimes a disc squishes out and its jelly presses on a nerve. That can make pain shoot down an arm or a leg.

Most of the time, this gets better with time, gentle exercise and medicine. Only some people need surgery.
levels.hs:
**Degenerative spine disease** means wear-and-tear changes in the spine that come with age. Almost everyone has some by middle age, and most people with changes on a scan have no symptoms at all.

**The parts:**
- **Intervertebral disc**: a tough outer ring (**annulus fibrosus**) around a jelly-like center (**nucleus pulposus**).
- **Facet joints**: small joints at the back of each level.
- **Ligaments**, including the ligamentum flavum behind the spinal canal.

**Common problems:**
- **Disc herniation**: the nucleus pushes through a tear in the annulus and presses on a nerve root. In the lower back this causes **sciatica**: pain shooting down the leg, sometimes with numbness or weakness.
- **Spinal stenosis**: narrowing of the canal from disc bulging, thick ligaments and enlarged facet joints. In the lumbar spine it causes **neurogenic claudication**: leg pain or heaviness on walking or standing, relieved by sitting or bending forward (like leaning on a shopping cart).
- **Spondylolisthesis**: one vertebra slipping forward on the one below.
- **Cervical myelopathy**: narrowing in the neck that squeezes the spinal cord, causing clumsy hands and an unsteady walk.

Most sciatica improves within weeks to a few months without surgery. Doctors watch for **red flags**, such as weakness that is getting worse, fever, cancer history or trouble controlling the bladder, which need urgent attention.
levels.college:
**Degenerative cascade.** Disc degeneration begins with loss of proteoglycans and water from the nucleus, reducing disc height. Load shifts to the facets, which develop arthritis and osteophytes. The ligamentum flavum buckles and thickens. Together these narrow the central canal, lateral recesses and foramina. Segmental instability can follow, producing degenerative spondylolisthesis, most often at L4-L5.

**Radiculopathy vs myelopathy.**
- **Radiculopathy** is nerve root compression: dermatomal pain, numbness, myotomal weakness, reduced reflexes (lower motor neuron signs).
- **Myelopathy** is spinal cord compression: hand clumsiness, gait imbalance, hyperreflexia, Hoffmann sign, upgoing plantar response (upper motor neuron signs). Degenerative cervical myelopathy is the most common cause of spinal cord dysfunction in adults.

**Which root?** In the lumbar spine, a typical **posterolateral** disc herniation at L4-L5 compresses the **traversing L5 root**; a **far lateral** herniation at the same level compresses the **exiting L4 root**. In the cervical spine, roots exit above their numbered vertebra, so a C5-C6 disc affects the C6 root.

- L4: knee reflex, ankle dorsiflexion, medial leg sensation.
- L5: big toe extension, hip abduction, top of foot.
- S1: ankle reflex, plantarflexion, lateral foot.

**Imaging.** MRI is the test of choice but must be matched to symptoms: disc bulges are present in a large share of pain-free people, rising with age. Flexion-extension radiographs show dynamic instability.

**Management.** Initial treatment is conservative: activity as tolerated, physiotherapy, pain relief, and sometimes epidural steroid injections. Surgery is considered for progressive or severe neurological deficit, cauda equina syndrome, myelopathy, or persistent disabling symptoms that match imaging after an adequate trial of conservative care.
levels.phd:
**Disc biology.** The adult nucleus pulposus is the largest avascular tissue in the body; its cells survive on diffusion through the cartilaginous endplates and live in a hypoxic, acidic, low-nutrient environment. Notochordal cells disappear in early life in humans, and their loss is associated with the onset of degeneration. Degeneration involves a shift from aggrecan and type II collagen synthesis toward catabolic enzymes (matrix metalloproteinases, ADAMTS) and inflammatory cytokines (IL-1, TNF-alpha). Nerve fibers and blood vessels then grow into fissured annulus, one theory for **discogenic pain**. Twin studies show degeneration is strongly heritable, with genetics explaining more of the variation than occupation.

**Why herniations hurt and then heal.** Radicular pain reflects both mechanical compression and chemical inflammation of the dorsal root ganglion by nucleus material. Many herniations, especially large sequestered fragments, shrink or disappear spontaneously through macrophage-driven resorption, which partly explains the favorable natural history.

**Imaging grades and their limits.** The Pfirrmann grading of disc degeneration and **Modic changes** (endplate marrow signal: type 1 edema, type 2 fat, type 3 sclerosis) are widely used. Modic type 1 changes have been linked to pain and a hypothesized low-grade infection by skin bacteria, but a large trial of antibiotic treatment did not show a clinically meaningful benefit.

**Myelopathy pathophysiology.** Static compression plus dynamic injury (repeated stretch and pinching in flexion and extension) and ischemia of the cord's microcirculation cause demyelination and neuron loss. High signal on T2-weighted MRI suggests edema or gliosis; low signal on T1 suggests irreversible damage and predicts worse outcome.

**Outcome research.** The SPORT trials showed that surgery gave faster and greater improvement than nonoperative care for disc herniation, stenosis and degenerative spondylolisthesis in as-treated analyses, but high crossover rates make intention-to-treat results harder to read.
levels.expert:
**The clinical question.** In degenerative disease the scan almost always shows "something." The surgeon's job is to decide whether the symptoms and examination match a specific compressive lesion, because operating on the wrong level or on pain that is not caused by the image is the classic failure.

**History and exam pearls.**
- Leg pain worse than back pain points to radiculopathy, which responds far better to surgery than isolated axial back pain.
- Neurogenic claudication improves with sitting and flexion; vascular claudication improves with standing still and comes with poor pulses. Check both.
- In older patients with "carpal tunnel," look for myelopathy: Hoffmann sign, brisk reflexes, poor tandem gait, and a hand that cannot open and close quickly.
- Document power by root carefully; foot drop timing matters for prognosis.

**Natural history and patience.** Most acute sciatica improves within six to twelve weeks. Early surgery mainly speeds recovery (Peul's 2007 trial: faster relief, similar results at one year), so the decision often depends on pain severity, work and patient preference. Severe or progressing weakness shifts the balance toward earlier surgery.

**Myelopathy is different.** Degenerative cervical myelopathy tends to worsen stepwise. Guidelines recommend surgery for moderate and severe myelopathy and offer it or close supervised follow-up for mild disease. Waiting until the patient cannot walk loses function that rarely returns.

**Red flags to never miss.** Cauda equina symptoms, progressive deficits, fever or infection risk (possible epidural abscess or discitis), history of cancer, unexplained weight loss, or major trauma.

**Shared decision-making.** Explain that surgery treats compression, not "a bad back." Set expectations clearly: leg pain relief is usually good; back pain may persist. The best outcomes come from the right patient, the right level and the right operation.

keyPoints: A disc has a tough outer annulus fibrosus and a jelly-like nucleus pulposus.
Radiculopathy (nerve root) gives lower motor neuron signs; myelopathy (spinal cord) gives upper motor neuron signs.
A posterolateral L4-L5 disc herniation compresses the traversing L5 root; a far lateral one hits L4.
Lumbar stenosis causes neurogenic claudication relieved by sitting or bending forward.
Most sciatica improves within weeks to months without surgery.
MRI findings are common in pain-free people, so they must match symptoms and exam.

advancedTest.q: A 45-year-old has right leg pain to the lateral foot, weak plantarflexion and an absent right ankle reflex. MRI shows a right posterolateral disc herniation. Most likely level?
advancedTest.explain: S1 signs from a posterolateral herniation point to L5-S1, where the traversing root is S1.

advancedTest.explain: Far lateral herniations sit in the foramen where the exiting root (L4) runs.

advancedTest.explain: Moderate or progressive degenerative cervical myelopathy is usually treated surgically to prevent further loss.

advancedTest.q: Which feature best distinguishes vascular from neurogenic claudication?
choices: Relief by simply standing still and weak foot pulses in vascular claudication
advancedTest.explain: Vascular claudication eases with rest even when standing; neurogenic needs flexion or sitting and pulses are normal.

lessons.title: Decompression

levels.kid:
When a nerve in the spine gets squished, it can hurt a lot or make a leg weak. **Decompression** surgery means giving the nerve more room, like loosening a shoe that's way too tight.

The surgeon makes a small cut in the back, uses a microscope, and carefully removes the bit that is pressing: a piece of squished disc, a thick band of tissue, or a bump of bone.

Once the nerve has space again, the shooting leg pain often gets better quickly. Many people walk around the same day or the next day.
levels.hs:
**Decompression** surgery relieves pressure on the spinal cord or nerve roots. The idea is simple: remove whatever is pressing and leave as much normal, stable spine as possible.

**Common operations:**
- **Microdiscectomy**: through a small incision, the surgeon removes the herniated piece of disc pressing on a nerve root. It is the standard surgery for sciatica that doesn't improve.
- **Laminectomy**: removal of the **lamina** (the back roof of the vertebra) and thickened ligament to widen the canal in spinal stenosis.
- **Laminotomy**: a smaller, partial removal of the lamina, keeping more of the bone.
- **Foraminotomy**: widening the **foramen**, the side opening where a nerve root leaves the spine.
- **ACDF** (anterior cervical discectomy and fusion): in the neck, the disc is removed from the front, the cord and roots are freed, and the level is fused.
- **Laminoplasty**: in the neck, the lamina is hinged open like a door to enlarge the canal while keeping motion.

**Risks:**
- a tear in the dura (the sac around the nerves) that can leak spinal fluid
- infection or bleeding
- nerve injury
- the disc herniating again at the same level
- instability if too much bone or joint is removed

Recovery after a microdiscectomy is often fast: leg pain can ease almost immediately, though numbness and weakness take longer to recover.
levels.college:
**Principle.** Decompress the neural elements adequately while preserving stability. The facet joints and pars interarticularis are key stabilizers; removing much of both facets, or the pars, risks iatrogenic instability and slippage.

**Lumbar disc surgery.** Microdiscectomy through a hemilaminotomy and flavectomy exposes the root, which is gently retracted to remove the herniated fragment. Removing only the fragment (sequestrectomy) versus more disc material is a trade-off between recurrent herniation and later disc collapse. Recurrence occurs in a minority of patients, roughly 5 to 15 percent in many series. Endoscopic discectomy is a less invasive alternative with similar outcomes in experienced hands.

**Lumbar stenosis.** Options include open laminectomy, bilateral decompression through a unilateral approach ("over-the-top"), and indirect decompression by restoring disc height with an interbody cage. The **Swedish Spinal Stenosis Study** (Försth, 2016) found that adding fusion to decompression did not improve outcomes, even in patients with degenerative spondylolisthesis. **SLIP** (Ghogawala, 2016) found a modest benefit from fusion for stable grade I spondylolisthesis. Practice now favors decompression alone for stable slips and fusion when there is clear instability.

**Cervical spine.** The choice between anterior and posterior approaches depends on where the compression is, the number of levels and the alignment:
- **Anterior** (ACDF, corpectomy) for disc-level compression and kyphosis.
- **Posterior** (laminoplasty, laminectomy with fusion) for multilevel compression in a lordotic spine, since the cord can drift back away from anterior pathology.
- **Posterior foraminotomy** for a single-root lateral disc or bony spur, avoiding fusion.

**Complications.** Incidental durotomy is the most common intraoperative problem; it is repaired primarily, and persistent leaks may cause headaches or a fluid collection. **C5 palsy**, deltoid and biceps weakness after cervical decompression, occurs in a small percentage and usually recovers over months.
levels.phd:
**Biomechanics of decompression.** Finite element and cadaver studies show that removing more than about half of each facet joint, or violating the pars, substantially increases segmental motion, particularly in flexion and rotation. Midline structures (the supraspinous and interspinous ligaments) also act as a posterior tension band; preserving them is the rationale for midline-sparing and unilateral bilateral decompression techniques. Postlaminectomy kyphosis is a particular risk in the cervical spine of children, whose growing spines depend on posterior elements, which is why laminoplasty is often preferred in younger patients.

**Recovery biology of the root.** Compression causes venous congestion, intraneural edema, impaired axonal transport and demyelination. Pain often responds rapidly to decompression because it is partly driven by inflammation and ectopic firing at the dorsal root ganglion. Motor recovery depends on the duration and severity of the deficit: complete foot drop of long duration recovers less well than a partial, recent deficit. Sensory loss and paresthesia often recover last, and some numbness may remain.

**Evidence questions.** The surgery-versus-conservative debate in sciatica has shifted from "whether" to "when": trials show faster relief with early surgery but convergence at one to two years. Cost-effectiveness depends on how much earlier return to work is valued. In lumbar stenosis, randomized trials show surgery outperforms nonoperative care at two to four years, though benefits narrow over time as the spine continues to degenerate.

**Minimally invasive and endoscopic techniques.** Tubular retractors and full-endoscopic systems reduce muscle disruption and length of stay in some studies, but comparative trials generally show similar long-term outcomes to open microsurgery. Their learning curve is steep. Augmented reality and navigation are being evaluated to improve accuracy in complex decompressions, but the main determinant of outcome remains correct patient and level selection.

**Ongoing research.** Annular closure devices aim to reduce reherniation after discectomy; biological disc repair and nucleus replacement remain experimental.
levels.expert:
**Thinking before you cut.** Ask three questions: what exactly is compressing which neural structure, is the segment stable, and what is the least destabilizing operation that fully decompresses it? An incomplete decompression and an unnecessary fusion are both common errors.

**Level and side.** Wrong-level surgery is a "never event." Confirm the level with intraoperative imaging after exposure, compare it with the counted levels on MRI (watch for transitional vertebrae such as a lumbarized S1), and mark the side in the consent and on the skin.

**Technique pearls.**
- In microdiscectomy, find the lateral edge of the root and the disc space before retracting; hidden sequestered fragments migrate up or down behind the vertebral body.
- In stenosis, decompress the lateral recesses where the traversing root is trapped under the facet, not just the central canal.
- Preserve at least half of each facet and the pars.
- Handle the dura gently. If you tear it, repair it watertight with sutures, sealant or a patch, and consider a period of flat bed rest.

**Cervical decisions.** For one or two disc levels with radiculopathy, ACDF or disc replacement is reliable. For multilevel myelopathy with preserved lordosis, laminoplasty preserves motion. Kyphosis pushes toward anterior surgery or posterior fusion that can correct alignment.

**After surgery.** Expect leg pain relief early; warn that numbness may linger. A new severe pain or deficit after an initial improvement suggests a hematoma or recurrent herniation and needs urgent MRI. A wound draining clear fluid suggests a CSF leak.

**Counseling.** Tell patients plainly: decompression treats nerve compression symptoms well and back pain much less predictably. Recurrent herniation can happen, and the rest of the spine keeps aging. Good outcomes come from honest expectations as much as from good technique.

keyPoints: Decompression removes what compresses the cord or roots while preserving stability.
Microdiscectomy removes a herniated disc fragment; laminectomy widens a stenotic canal.
Removing too much facet joint or the pars risks iatrogenic instability.
The Swedish Spinal Stenosis Study found adding fusion to decompression did not improve outcomes.
Incidental durotomy is the most common intraoperative complication and is repaired primarily.
C5 palsy is a recognized, usually temporary, complication of cervical decompression.

lessons.title: Instrumentation & Fusion

levels.kid:
Sometimes spine bones wiggle too much, or slip out of line, and that hurts and pinches nerves. Then surgeons can do a **fusion**: they make two or more spine bones grow together into one solid piece.

To hold the bones still while they heal, surgeons use special metal **screws** and **rods**, like the frame that holds a young tree straight. They also pack in bits of bone, which act like seeds so new bone grows across the gap.

After a few months, the bones knit together. The metal usually just stays inside quietly.
levels.hs:
**Spinal fusion** joins two or more vertebrae so they heal into one solid bone and stop moving at that level. **Instrumentation** is the hardware that holds everything steady while the bone heals.

**When is fusion used?**
- **Instability**: abnormal movement, for example after a fracture or a slip (spondylolisthesis) that moves on bending
- **Deformity**: scoliosis (sideways curve) or kyphosis (forward hunch)
- Trauma, tumors and infections that destroy bone
- After decompression that had to remove stabilizing structures

**The hardware:**
- **Pedicle screws** go through the pedicles (bony bridges at the back of each vertebra) into the vertebral body, then connect to **rods**.
- **Interbody cages** replace the disc, restoring height and giving bone a place to fuse. They can be inserted from the back (PLIF, TLIF), the front (ALIF) or the side (lateral approaches).
- In the neck, plates and screws are used after anterior discectomy.

**Bone graft** is what actually fuses: the patient's own bone (autograft), donor bone (allograft) or bone substitutes.

**Risks** include screws placed in the wrong spot, infection, the bones failing to fuse (**pseudarthrosis**) and **adjacent segment disease**, extra wear at the levels next to the fusion. Smoking makes fusion much less likely to succeed.
levels.college:
**Biology of fusion.** A successful arthrodesis needs three things: osteogenic cells, an osteoconductive scaffold and osteoinductive signals, plus mechanical stability. **Iliac crest autograft** provides all three and remains the reference standard, but harvest causes donor-site pain. Local bone from the decompression, allograft, ceramics and demineralized bone matrix are common alternatives. Recombinant bone morphogenetic protein is osteoinductive but has been linked to complications such as soft-tissue swelling in the anterior neck, so its use is selective. Wolff's law applies: bone remodels in response to load, and rigid fixation plus load sharing through an interbody graft promotes fusion.

**Instrumentation.**
- **Pedicle screws** give three-column fixation and are the workhorse of thoracolumbar surgery. Placement uses anatomical landmarks, fluoroscopy, CT navigation or robotics; breaches medially or inferiorly threaten nerve roots and the dura.
- **Interbody techniques**: PLIF and TLIF from posterior; ALIF through the abdomen for large cages and lordosis restoration at L4-S1; LLIF/XLIF through the psoas (risk to the lumbar plexus, monitored with EMG); OLIF anterior to the psoas.
- **Cervical**: anterior plates; posterior lateral mass screws in the subaxial spine; C1-C2 fixation for atlantoaxial instability.
- **Cervical disc arthroplasty** is a motion-preserving alternative to ACDF in selected one- or two-level disease.

**Sagittal alignment.** Outcomes in adult deformity correlate with spinopelvic parameters: **pelvic incidence** (a fixed anatomical angle) should roughly match lumbar lordosis within about 10 degrees; pelvic tilt and the **sagittal vertical axis** reflect compensation. Fusing a spine in too little lordosis ("flatback") causes pain and fatigue.

**Complications.** Pseudarthrosis (risk factors: smoking, diabetes, osteoporosis, multilevel fusion), hardware failure, adjacent segment degeneration, proximal junctional kyphosis after long deformity fusions, infection and malpositioned screws.
levels.phd:
**History.** Hibbs and Albee described spinal fusion in 1911, initially for tuberculosis of the spine. **Paul Harrington's** distraction rods (1960s) made correction of scoliosis possible; Roy-Camille and others popularized pedicle screws in the 1970s and 1980s, enabling segmental three-column control. Each advance traded one problem for another: Harrington rods corrected curves but flattened lumbar lordosis, producing iatrogenic flatback syndrome and teaching the field that sagittal balance matters as much as coronal correction.

**Biomechanics.** Pedicle screw pullout strength depends on bone density, thread design, screw diameter and length, and insertion trajectory. **Cortical bone trajectory** screws engage denser cortical bone in a medial-to-lateral path, useful in osteoporosis. Cement augmentation increases fixation in osteoporotic bone. Rod material and stiffness influence load sharing; very stiff constructs may accelerate adjacent-level stress, while less stiff ones risk nonunion. Whether adjacent segment disease is caused by fusion or simply reflects the natural history of a degenerating spine remains debated; studies of motion-preserving arthroplasty suggest a modest reduction in reoperation at adjacent levels.

**Alignment science.** Jean Dubousset's "cone of economy" frames posture as maintaining the head over the pelvis with minimal muscular effort. Schwab's SRS classification uses PI-LL mismatch, pelvic tilt and sagittal vertical axis; later age-adjusted targets and the GAP score recognized that older patients tolerate, and may need, different alignment goals. Overcorrection in the elderly increases proximal junctional failure.

**Enabling technologies.** Intraoperative CT navigation and robotic guidance report high screw accuracy and lower radiation to staff, but evidence that they improve clinical outcomes is still limited. Patient-specific rods and 3D-printed titanium cages with porous surfaces are designed to encourage bone ingrowth. Research into osteobiologics continues, but none has fully matched autograft across all settings.
levels.expert:
**Should this patient be fused?** Fusion is a reconstruction, not a pain operation. Strong indications are instability, deformity, and structural destruction. Fusion for isolated degenerative back pain without instability has modest benefit at best, and failed fusion operations are a major cause of chronic disability.

**Preoperative optimization.**
- Stop smoking and nicotine products: nonunion risk rises sharply.
- Check and treat **osteoporosis** (DEXA or CT bone density); weak bone loosens screws.
- Control diabetes and nutrition; screen for infection.
- Obtain standing full-length radiographs in deformity cases and calculate pelvic incidence, lumbar lordosis, pelvic tilt and SVA.

**Intraoperative pearls.**
- Know pedicle anatomy at every level; thoracic pedicles are narrow and lie close to the cord.
- Use neuromonitoring (motor and sensory evoked potentials, triggered EMG for screw testing) in deformity and thoracic cases.
- Prepare the endplates and fusion bed carefully: fusion depends on biology, not metal.
- Restore lordosis with the interbody graft and rod contour; do not leave a patient fused in kyphosis.
- In long constructs, take care with the top level to reduce proximal junctional kyphosis.

**Postoperative pitfalls.**
- New radicular pain or weakness: suspect a malpositioned screw or cage; obtain CT and revise early if it is in the wrong place.
- Persistent pain beyond a year with a lucent halo around screws or motion on films: suspect pseudarthrosis; consider infection, including low-grade organisms.
- Adjacent segment problems may appear years later; counsel patients beforehand.

**Senior perspective.** The best spine surgeons fuse less often and plan alignment more carefully. Ask what the spine will look like in ten years, not just whether the screws look good today.

keyPoints: Fusion makes vertebrae heal into one solid bone; instrumentation holds them still while they heal.
Main indications: instability, deformity, trauma, tumors and infection.
Pedicle screws and rods are the workhorse; interbody cages replace the disc (PLIF, TLIF, ALIF, LLIF).
Iliac crest autograft is the reference graft; smoking and osteoporosis raise nonunion risk.
Pelvic incidence should roughly match lumbar lordosis; flatback causes pain and fatigue.
Complications include pseudarthrosis, malpositioned screws and adjacent segment disease.

test.explain: Adjacent levels take more stress and keep degenerating.

test.q: Which graft is considered the reference standard for fusion?
test.explain: Autograft provides cells, scaffold and signals.

test.q: A sideways curvature of the spine is called ___.
test.explain: Scoliosis is coronal-plane deformity.

test.q: Which fixed anatomical pelvic angle is matched to lumbar lordosis in deformity planning?
test.explain: Pelvic incidence is constant for each adult and guides how much lordosis is needed.

test.q: In XLIF, the surgeon passes through the ___ muscle, risking the lumbar plexus.
test.explain: The lateral transpsoas approach requires EMG monitoring of the plexus.

test.q: Whose rods (1960s) first made scoliosis correction possible?
test.explain: Harrington distraction rods corrected curves but flattened lumbar lordosis.

kidTest.q: Spinal fusion makes spine bones:
kidTest.explain: Fusion joins bones into one solid piece.

kidTest.q: What holds the bones still while they heal?
kidTest.explain: Screws and rods act like a frame.

kidTest.q: Bits of bone packed in work like:
kidTest.explain: Bone graft helps new bone grow across.

kidTest.explain: Bone healing takes months.

kidTest.explain: Fuse means join together.

kidTest.q: Does smoking help bones heal?

advancedTest.q: Ten days after L4-L5 TLIF, a patient has new right L5 radicular pain and weakness. CT shows the right L5 pedicle screw breaching medially. Best management?
choices: Remove all hardware and not fuse
Start a stronger pain medicine only
advancedTest.explain: A symptomatic malpositioned screw should be revised promptly to relieve the root.

advancedTest.q: An adult deformity patient has pelvic incidence of 60 degrees and lumbar lordosis of 30 degrees with high pelvic tilt. What does this indicate?
choices: PI-LL mismatch with compensatory pelvic retroversion
advancedTest.explain: A 30-degree mismatch means loss of lordosis; the pelvis rotates backward to compensate.

advancedTest.q: Why is anterior cervical BMP use limited?
choices: It has been linked to dangerous soft-tissue swelling in the neck
advancedTest.explain: Prevertebral swelling can compromise swallowing and the airway.

advancedTest.q: A patient has back pain 18 months after fusion; films show a lucent halo around screws and motion across the level. Which two diagnoses must be considered?
advancedTest.explain: Loosening suggests nonunion, and low-grade infection is a known cause of loosening.

lessons.title: Spinal Trauma

levels.kid:
Your spine protects your spinal cord, the big cable that carries messages between your brain and your body. A bad crash or fall can break spine bones.

If someone might have hurt their neck or back, helpers keep them very still, often with a stiff collar, so a broken bone can't move and hurt the cord.

At the hospital, doctors take pictures, check if the person can feel and move their arms and legs, and decide what to do. Some breaks heal in a brace. Others need surgery with screws and rods to hold the spine steady and take pressure off the cord.
levels.hs:
**Spinal trauma** ranges from stable fractures that heal in a brace to unstable injuries that damage the spinal cord. Common causes are car crashes, falls (especially in older adults), sports and diving into shallow water.

**First steps:**
- Follow trauma priorities: airway, breathing, circulation.
- Keep the spine protected, with a collar for the neck and careful log-rolling.
- Clinical rules (such as NEXUS and the Canadian C-spine rule) decide who needs imaging; **CT** is the main test for bone, **MRI** for the cord, discs and ligaments.

**Grading spinal cord injury:** the **ASIA Impairment Scale** runs from A to E:
- **A**: complete, no movement or feeling below the injury, including the lowest sacral segments
- **B to D**: incomplete injuries with increasing function
- **E**: normal

**Classic injuries:**
- **Jefferson fracture**: a burst of the C1 ring
- **Hangman's fracture**: through both sides of C2
- **Odontoid fractures**: of the peg of C2
- **Burst fractures** and **Chance fractures** (from a lap seatbelt) in the thoracolumbar spine

**Central cord syndrome** is the most common incomplete injury: the arms are weaker than the legs, often after a hyperextension injury in an older person with a narrow neck canal.

Surgery stabilizes unstable fractures and decompresses the cord. Blood pressure is kept up to protect the injured cord.
levels.college:
**Stability frameworks.** Denis' **three-column model** (anterior, middle, posterior) underlies the idea that injury to two or more columns is usually unstable. Modern systems combine morphology, ligament integrity and neurology:
- **TLICS** (thoracolumbar): morphology (compression, burst, translation/rotation, distraction), posterior ligamentous complex integrity, and neurological status. Total of 3 or less suggests nonoperative care, 5 or more suggests surgery, and 4 is either.
- **SLIC** for the subaxial cervical spine uses a similar logic.
- **AO Spine classification**: type A compression, type B tension band failure, type C translation, with neurological and patient modifiers.

**Upper cervical injuries.**
- **Odontoid fractures** (Anderson-D'Alonzo): type I tip, type II base of the dens (highest nonunion risk, especially in older adults), type III extending into the body (usually heals in a brace).
- **Atlanto-occipital dislocation**: often fatal; diagnosed by measuring the craniocervical relationship on CT.

**Spinal cord syndromes.**
- **Central cord**: arms more than legs, often without fracture.
- **Anterior cord**: loss of motor function and pain/temperature with preserved proprioception (dorsal columns spared).
- **Brown-Séquard**: same-side weakness and proprioception loss, opposite-side pain and temperature loss.

**Shock.** **Neurogenic shock** (hypotension with bradycardia from loss of sympathetic tone, injuries at T6 and above) differs from **spinal shock** (temporary loss of reflexes below the injury). Hemorrhage must always be excluded first in a hypotensive trauma patient.

**Management.** Early decompression and stabilization: the STASCIS study found that decompression within 24 hours was associated with better neurological recovery, and later guidelines support early surgery. Guidelines commonly advise keeping mean arterial pressure around 85 to 90 mmHg for several days. High-dose steroids for acute spinal cord injury are controversial and no longer routine.
levels.phd:
**Primary and secondary injury.** The primary mechanical injury (contusion, compression, laceration) is followed by a cascade of **secondary injury**: hemorrhage and microvascular failure, ischemia, glutamate excitotoxicity, calcium influx, free-radical damage, inflammation, and apoptosis of oligodendrocytes extending over days to weeks. A glial and fibrotic scar forms around a fluid-filled cyst. Secondary injury is the window for neuroprotection, which is why time to decompression and perfusion are emphasized.

**Neuroprotection trials.** The NASCIS trials of methylprednisolone generated decades of controversy: subgroup and timing analyses suggested modest benefit, while critics pointed to post-hoc analyses and increased infections and other complications. Current guidelines do not recommend it routinely. Riluzole, a sodium channel blocker, was tested in a phase III trial (RISCIS) that did not meet its primary endpoint, though some secondary analyses were encouraging. Hypothermia, minocycline and other agents remain investigational.

**Spinal cord perfusion.** Intraspinal pressure monitoring studies showed that a swollen cord compressed against the dura behaves like a compartment, and that spinal cord perfusion pressure, not just mean arterial pressure, may better predict outcome. Expansion duraplasty is being studied (DISCUS trial) to relieve this.

**Regeneration research.** Barriers include myelin-associated inhibitors (Nogo-A, MAG), chondroitin sulfate proteoglycans in the scar, and the low intrinsic growth capacity of adult central neurons. Strategies include anti-Nogo antibodies, chondroitinase, cell transplantation and biomaterial bridges. **Epidural electrical stimulation** combined with intensive rehabilitation has enabled some people with chronic injuries to stand or take steps, and brain-spine interfaces that link cortical recordings to stimulation have shown proof of concept. These are not yet cures, and outcomes vary widely.

**Predicting recovery.** The single best early predictor is whether the injury is complete or incomplete at an examination done after spinal shock settles; preserved pinprick sensation in the sacral segments predicts much better motor recovery.
levels.expert:
**Assessment priorities.** In the trauma bay, a spinal injury never takes priority over airway, breathing and bleeding. A hypotensive patient is bleeding until proven otherwise, even with obvious paralysis. After stabilization, perform and document an **ISNCSCI exam**: motor levels, sensory levels, and the sacral exam (anal sensation and voluntary contraction), which determines whether the injury is complete.

**Imaging pearls.**
- CT the whole spine when one fracture is found; noncontiguous fractures are common.
- Obtain MRI for neurological deficits, suspected ligament injury, or when the exam does not match CT.
- In ankylosed spines (ankylosing spondylitis, DISH), even minor falls cause unstable fractures through fused bone; treat them as unstable and image the whole spine.

**Decision-making.**
- Use TLICS or AO criteria, but remember that an intact posterior ligamentous complex can allow a burst fracture without deficit to be treated in a brace.
- Incomplete injury with ongoing compression: decompress early, ideally within 24 hours.
- Type II odontoid in an older patient: weigh surgery against collar, as nonunion is common but surgery carries risk; many end up with a stable fibrous union.
- Central cord syndrome without instability: modern evidence supports earlier surgery than once thought when there is persistent compression.

**Critical care.** Maintain mean arterial pressure targets, often with vasopressors, and avoid hypoxia. High cervical injuries risk respiratory failure: watch vital capacity closely, as fatigue can develop over the first days. Prevent pressure injuries and blood clots, and manage the bladder from day one.

**Communication.** Families want to know if the patient will walk. Be honest that early prognosis is uncertain, explain what the sacral exam means, and avoid false hope or premature finality in the first days.

**Long view.** Rehabilitation determines much of the eventual quality of life. Connect patients early with specialist spinal cord injury rehabilitation.

keyPoints: Spinal trauma care starts with airway, breathing and circulation; the spine is protected throughout.
The ASIA Impairment Scale grades cord injury from A (complete) to E (normal).
TLICS scores morphology, posterior ligament integrity and neurology: 3 or less nonoperative, 5 or more surgery.
Central cord syndrome causes arm weakness worse than leg weakness, often after hyperextension in older adults.
Neurogenic shock is hypotension with bradycardia; bleeding must be excluded first.
Early decompression (within 24 hours) and blood pressure support are associated with better recovery.

test.q: What are the first priorities in a patient with possible spinal trauma?
choices: Airway, breathing and circulation with spine protection
test.explain: Trauma resuscitation comes first while the spine is protected.

test.q: ASIA Impairment Scale grade A means:
choices: Complete injury with no sacral sparing
test.explain: Grade A is complete: no motor or sensory function in the lowest sacral segments.

test.q: A burst fracture of the C1 ring is called a:
test.explain: Jefferson described the C1 burst; hangman's fracture is through C2.

test.q: Which odontoid fracture type has the highest risk of nonunion?
test.explain: Type II at the base of the dens has poor blood supply and high nonunion, especially in older adults.

test.q: Weak arms with relatively strong legs after a neck hyperextension injury in an older adult suggests:
test.explain: Central cord syndrome is the most common incomplete cord injury.

test.q: Low blood pressure plus slow heart rate after a high spinal cord injury suggests:
test.explain: Loss of sympathetic tone causes hypotension and bradycardia, but bleeding must still be excluded.

test.q: A TLICS score of 6 usually suggests:
test.explain: Scores of 5 or more generally favor surgical stabilization.

test.q: A Chance fracture is classically caused by:
choices: A fall on an outstretched hand
test.explain: Flexion over a lap belt distracts the posterior elements; check for abdominal injuries too.

test.q: Brown-Séquard syndrome causes loss of pain and temperature on the ___ side.
test.explain: The spinothalamic tract crosses near entry, so pain and temperature loss is contralateral.

test.q: Which imaging test is best for the spinal cord and ligaments?
test.explain: CT shows bone best; MRI shows cord, discs and ligaments.

test.q: The STASCIS study supported decompression within ___ hours of injury.
test.explain: Early decompression was associated with better neurological recovery.

test.q: What letter on the ASIA scale means normal function?
test.explain: ASIA E means normal motor and sensory function.

kidTest.q: The spinal cord is like a:
kidTest.explain: It carries messages between brain and body.

kidTest.q: If someone might have hurt their neck, helpers should:
kidTest.explain: Keeping still protects the spinal cord.

kidTest.q: What do helpers often put on the neck?
kidTest.explain: A collar keeps the neck from moving.

kidTest.q: Some spine breaks heal in a:
kidTest.explain: A brace holds the spine still while it heals.

kidTest.q: Surgeons can hold a broken spine steady with screws and ___.
kidTest.explain: Screws and rods act like a frame.

kidTest.q: Can diving into shallow water cause spine injuries?
kidTest.explain: Always check water depth before diving.

advancedTest.q: A 75-year-old with ankylosing spondylitis falls from standing and has neck pain but a normal exam. CT shows a subtle fracture through a fused segment. Correct approach?
choices: Treat as highly unstable and image the whole spine
advancedTest.explain: Fractures through ankylosed spines are typically unstable and often multiple.

advancedTest.q: After a cervical injury, a patient has no motor function below C6 but preserved pinprick sensation around the anus. Which grade and prognosis?
choices: ASIA B, better chance of motor recovery
advancedTest.explain: Sacral sensory sparing makes it incomplete (B), with meaningfully better recovery odds, especially with preserved pinprick.

advancedTest.q: A trauma patient with a T4 cord injury has blood pressure 70/40 and heart rate 125. Most likely cause?
advancedTest.explain: Tachycardia argues against pure neurogenic shock; find and stop the bleeding.

advancedTest.q: Why is spinal cord perfusion pressure being studied rather than only mean arterial pressure?
choices: Spinal cords have no blood supply
The swollen cord against the dura can raise intraspinal pressure, reducing perfusion
advancedTest.explain: A compartment-like rise in intraspinal pressure means MAP alone may overestimate cord perfusion.

lessons.title: Cauda Equina & Emergencies

levels.kid:
At the bottom of your spine, the spinal cord ends and splits into lots of nerves that look like a horse's tail. Doctors call this the **cauda equina**, which means "horse's tail" in Latin.

These nerves help your legs move and help you control when you go to the bathroom. If something squeezes them hard, like a big squished disc, that is an emergency.

Warning signs are both legs hurting or going weak, numbness in the seat area, and trouble peeing. Then doctors do a scan right away, and surgeons operate fast to free the nerves before they get hurt for good.
levels.hs:
Some spine problems can't wait. These are **spinal emergencies**, where hours can decide whether someone keeps the ability to walk or control their bladder.

**Cauda equina syndrome (CES)**
The spinal cord ends around the L1-L2 level. Below that, the nerve roots for the legs, bladder and bowel hang down like a horse's tail, the **cauda equina**. A large central disc herniation is the most common cause of compression. Warning signs:
- back pain with sciatica in **both** legs
- **saddle numbness**: reduced feeling around the buttocks and inner thighs, where you'd sit on a saddle
- difficulty starting to pee, or not feeling the bladder fill
- leg weakness
CES needs an **emergency MRI** and urgent surgery to decompress the nerves.

**Other emergencies:**
- **Spinal epidural abscess**: infection in the spinal canal, causing back pain, fever and then weakness. Needs antibiotics and often surgery.
- **Metastatic spinal cord compression**: cancer spreading to the spine and pressing on the cord. Treated with steroids, radiation and often surgery.
- **Spinal epidural hematoma**: a blood clot pressing on the cord, often in people on blood thinners.

Doctors teach patients with back pain these red-flag symptoms so they come straight to the hospital if they appear, rather than waiting.
levels.college:
**Anatomy.** The conus medullaris usually ends at L1-L2 in adults. Below it, the lumbar and sacral roots form the cauda equina. Sacral roots S2-S4 control bladder and bowel function and supply perineal sensation.

**Cauda equina syndrome.**
- **Causes**: large central disc herniation (most common, often at L4-L5 or L5-S1), tumor, abscess, hematoma, trauma, and complications of spinal procedures.
- **Stages**: **CES-I** (incomplete: altered urinary sensation or difficulty voiding, but still controlled) and **CES-R** (retention with overflow). Outcomes are much better when surgery happens before retention.
- **Assessment**: perineal sensation, anal tone and voluntary contraction, and a post-void residual bladder scan. Symptoms are unreliable alone, and the exam can be normal early, so a low threshold for MRI is essential.
- **Timing**: meta-analyses (Ahn, 2000) found better outcomes with decompression within 48 hours; many surgeons operate as soon as possible after diagnosis, particularly in incomplete CES.

**Conus medullaris vs cauda equina.** Conus lesions cause early, symmetric sphincter dysfunction with mixed upper and lower motor neuron signs and less radicular pain. Cauda equina lesions are lower motor neuron, often asymmetric, with severe radicular pain.

**Metastatic spinal cord compression (MSCC).** Commonest with lung, breast, prostate, kidney and myeloma. Back pain is usually the first symptom, often for weeks before weakness. Corticosteroids (dexamethasone) reduce edema. **Patchell's 2005 trial** showed that decompressive surgery plus radiotherapy kept more patients walking than radiotherapy alone in selected patients. The **NOMS** framework (neurological, oncological, mechanical, systemic) and the **SINS** score for instability guide treatment.

**Spinal epidural abscess.** Risk factors include diabetes, bloodstream infection, recent spinal procedures and immune suppression. *Staphylococcus aureus* is the usual organism. The classic triad of back pain, fever and neurological deficit is present in only a minority at presentation; MRI with contrast confirms it.
levels.phd:
**Why time matters in CES.** Nerve roots of the cauda equina have a relatively poor blood supply, with a watershed zone in the proximal third of the root. Compression causes venous congestion, intraneural edema, impaired nutrient diffusion from CSF and ischemia. Animal experiments show that both the pressure and the speed of onset matter: rapid compression causes more dysfunction than gradual compression at the same pressure. This supports urgent decompression, although clinical evidence is limited to observational studies, which are confounded because patients with more severe CES are often operated on fastest.

**The diagnostic problem.** CES is uncommon, but back pain with sciatica is very common, and many patients with suspected CES have negative MRIs. The positive predictive value of individual symptoms is low. Missed or delayed diagnosis is a leading cause of medicolegal claims in spinal surgery. Health systems are therefore debating rapid-access MRI pathways and safety-net advice, accepting a large number of negative scans to avoid missing true cases.

**Long-term outcomes.** Even after timely surgery, some patients have persistent bladder, bowel and sensory symptoms and chronic pain. Outcome research increasingly uses patient-reported measures and recognizes the psychological burden of persistent symptoms.

**Spinal oncology revolution.** Stereotactic body radiotherapy (SBRT) delivers high-dose, conformal radiation to spinal metastases, achieving durable local control even for traditionally radioresistant tumors such as renal cell carcinoma and melanoma. This has led to **separation surgery**: rather than aggressively removing the tumor, surgeons create a margin of a few millimeters between tumor and cord, stabilize the spine, and let SBRT control the tumor. The epidural spinal cord compression (Bilsky) grade helps decide when separation is needed.

**Infection biology.** Epidural abscess reflects both direct compression and septic thrombophlebitis or arteritis that can cause cord infarction, which explains why some patients deteriorate faster than the compression alone predicts.
levels.expert:
**Mindset.** In spinal emergencies, the cost of missing the diagnosis is far greater than the cost of a negative scan. A senior surgeon's habit is to ask about bladder, bowel and saddle symptoms in every patient with back pain and sciatica, and to document the answers.

**Cauda equina in practice.**
- Ask specifically about altered urinary sensation, straining to void, and saddle numbness, in plain language the patient understands.
- Examine perineal sensation to light touch and pinprick, and assess anal tone; scan the bladder after voiding.
- Get an MRI urgently, at night if necessary. Do not wait for retention to develop.
- If MRI confirms compression in a symptomatic patient, decompress promptly with a wide laminectomy and careful removal of the fragment; central discs may need bilateral exposure to avoid pulling on the compressed roots.
- Counsel honestly: recovery of bladder function may be incomplete, especially if retention was present.

**Metastatic compression.**
- Start steroids promptly once the diagnosis is made, coordinate with oncology, and use NOMS.
- Radiosensitive tumors (myeloma, lymphoma) without instability may be treated with radiation alone.
- Instability (high SINS) or radioresistant tumors with high-grade compression favor surgery and stabilization followed by SBRT.
- Consider prognosis and the patient's goals; a long reconstruction is not right for a patient with only weeks to live.

**Epidural abscess.**
- Take blood cultures and, unless the patient is septic, consider holding antibiotics briefly until an organism sample is obtained.
- Patients with neurological deficits generally need surgical drainage; nonoperative treatment with close monitoring may suit selected patients without deficits, but deterioration can be sudden.

**Hematoma.** Reverse anticoagulation quickly and decompress if there is a deficit.

**Never forget.** Write down the time of symptom onset and of each exam; these timelines guide decisions and protect patients.

keyPoints: The cauda equina is the bundle of lumbar and sacral nerve roots below the conus (about L1-L2).
Red flags: bilateral sciatica, saddle numbness, urinary difficulty or retention, leg weakness.
Suspected cauda equina syndrome needs an emergency MRI and urgent decompression.
Outcomes are better if surgery happens before urinary retention (CES-I rather than CES-R).
Metastatic cord compression: steroids, radiation, and surgery plus radiation for selected patients (Patchell).
Spinal epidural abscess classically causes back pain, fever and deficits; the full triad is often absent.

test.q: Where does the adult spinal cord usually end?
test.explain: The conus medullaris ends around L1-L2; below it lie the cauda equina roots.

test.q: Which symptom is a red flag for cauda equina syndrome?
test.explain: Saddle numbness reflects compression of sacral roots.

test.q: What is the first test for suspected cauda equina syndrome?
test.explain: MRI shows the compression and guides urgent surgery.

test.q: CES-R means cauda equina syndrome with:
test.explain: CES-R has painless urinary retention with overflow; outcomes are worse than CES-I.

test.q: The most common cause of cauda equina syndrome is:
test.explain: A big central disc compresses many roots at once.

test.q: Patchell's 2005 trial showed that for selected metastatic cord compression patients:
choices: Surgery plus radiotherapy kept more patients walking than radiotherapy alone
test.explain: Decompressive surgery plus radiation improved ambulation in selected patients.

test.q: Which organism most often causes spinal epidural abscess?
test.explain: S. aureus is the usual cause.

test.q: Compared with cauda equina lesions, conus medullaris lesions typically cause:
choices: Early symmetric sphincter problems with less radicular pain
test.explain: Conus lesions affect sacral cord segments early and symmetrically.

test.q: Cauda equina means 'horse's ___' in Latin.
test.explain: The spray of nerve roots looks like a horse's tail.

test.q: Name the steroid commonly started for metastatic spinal cord compression.
test.explain: Dexamethasone reduces cord edema while definitive treatment is arranged.

test.q: A bladder scan after urination measures the post-void ___.
test.explain: A high post-void residual suggests retention.

test.q: Within how many hours did Ahn's 2000 meta-analysis find better outcomes from CES decompression?
test.explain: Decompression within 48 hours was associated with better outcomes, and many surgeons aim to operate sooner.

kidTest.q: Cauda equina means:
kidTest.explain: The nerves look like a horse's tail.

kidTest.q: These nerves help with:
choices: Moving legs and going to the bathroom
kidTest.explain: They control legs, bladder and bowel.

kidTest.q: If these nerves get squeezed hard, it is:
kidTest.explain: Fast surgery protects the nerves.

kidTest.q: Which is a warning sign?
choices: Trouble peeing with back and leg pain
kidTest.explain: Bathroom trouble with back pain needs a doctor right away.

kidTest.q: Doctors check the nerves quickly with a special ___.
kidTest.explain: An MRI scan shows what's pressing on the nerves.

kidTest.q: Should someone with these warning signs wait a week?
choices: No, go to the hospital right away
kidTest.explain: Hours matter for saving nerve function.

advancedTest.q: A 40-year-old with sciatica now reports difficulty starting to urinate and reduced sensation when wiping, but can still control his bladder. Post-void residual is mildly raised. MRI shows a large central L5-S1 disc. Best plan?
choices: Urgent decompression, as this is CES-I
advancedTest.explain: Incomplete CES has the best outcomes with prompt surgery before retention.

advancedTest.q: A patient with metastatic myeloma has mild epidural compression, no instability and no deficit. Most appropriate initial treatment?
advancedTest.explain: Myeloma is radiosensitive; without instability or high-grade compression, radiation is first-line.

advancedTest.q: Why is separation surgery combined with SBRT for radioresistant metastases?
choices: Separation surgery removes all cancer cells
Surgery creates a small margin from the cord so high-dose SBRT can safely control the tumor
advancedTest.explain: A margin between tumor and cord lets SBRT deliver a high dose without injuring the cord.

advancedTest.q: A diabetic patient has severe back pain and fever, then rapidly develops leg weakness worse than the MRI compression seems to explain. Which mechanism may explain this?
choices: Septic thrombophlebitis or arteritis causing cord ischemia
advancedTest.explain: Vascular involvement can infarct the cord beyond the compressive effect.
